approved: Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (2019 Measures No. 1) Bill 2019
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would clarify how public interest immunity applies to continuing detention order applications for terrorist offenders.

The AFP minister would have to notify a terrorist offender in writing when information is excluded from a CDO application due to public interest immunity, and the offender could then seek access to that information.
The bill states that a terrorist offender who seeks access to such information would not be required to prove to the court that the immunity claim should not be upheld.
Clarifies the operation of public interest immunity in relation to continuing detention order applications.
Requires the AFP minister to give written notice to a terrorist offender when information is excluded on the basis of public interest immunity.
Specifies that a terrorist offender seeking access to excluded information does not have to satisfy the court that the immunity claim should not be upheld.
Terrorist offenders subject to continuing detention order applications, the AFP minister, and relevant operational agencies.

Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (2019 Measures No. 1) Bill 2019 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea

The bill introduces a presumption against bail and parole for individuals who have supported or been linked to terrorist activities, and makes two amendments to improve the continuing detention order scheme for high-risk terrorist offenders. The measures follow a COAG agreement and recommendations from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor, with the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security unanimously recommending passage.

Labor supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (2019 Measures No. 1) Bill 2019, which aligns with Council of Australian Governments principles from 5 October 2017 on bail and parole for terror-linked offenders and addresses a gap in continuing detention orders. The government accepted a Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security recommendation, but Labor and Liberal members disagreed on one issue relating to Australia's obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
